chapters.title: A letter from the seaside
chapters.src: Letter to Manmatha Nath Bhattacharya, U.S.A., 5 September 1894 (translated from Bengali)
lines: September eighteen ninety-four. Swami Vivekananda has been in America for just over a year.
He writes in Bengali to a friend in Madras, Manmatha Nath Bhattacharya.
His friend has asked about a weaving machine, and the Swami promises to make inquiries and let him know.
For now he is resting at Annisquam, a village on the seacoast of Massachusetts.

lines.q: Some come to bathe in the sea, some to take rest, and some to catch husbands.

lines: What follows is one of his most candid letters: America and India, seen side by side.

chapters.title: A strong sense of decorum
lines: There is a strong sense of decorum in this country, he writes.
In the presence of women you must always be covered from neck to foot, and the body's normal functions are never mentioned.
You may blow your nose a thousand times into a handkerchief, but to belch is highly uncivilised.
A low-cut evening gown is acceptable, yet to go barefoot is as bad as being naked.

lines.q: Just as we always dwell on the soul, so they take care of the body.

lines: There is no end to the cleaning and embellishing of it, and one who fails to do this has no place in society.

chapters.title: Cow-dung and spotless plates
lines: To Americans, cooking over cow-dung fuel and eating on the floor is eating like pigs. The very word is taboo in English.
Yet many will drink from the same glass without washing it, and rarely wash things before cooking.
But if the cook's clothes are a little soiled, she is thrown out.
The table-ware is all spick and span.

lines.q: They are the richest people on earth; their enjoyments and luxuries beggar description.

chapters.title: Visit the next village
lines: In Rajputana, he notes, people dine on a low seat with the plate on a low table, far better than a banana leaf on an earthen floor.
Bengali women lose caste if they wear shoes; Rajput women lose caste if they do not. And Manu says, one shall always wear shoes.
People should have a decent standard of living: neat and clean, even if not luxurious.

lines.q: Why do we have to be Englishmen? It is enough for the present if we imitate our brothers of the western provinces.

lines: If group after group of Indians travel the world and come back, the face of India will change within twenty years.
But how will anything happen if the people of one village do not visit the next? By and by, he writes, the stubborn Bengali boys will awaken the country.

chapters.title: The root of all sins
lines: Then he turns, sharply, to child marriage.

lines.q: Manmatha Babu, you will have to stop this shameful business of marrying off nine-year-old girls. That is the root of all sins.

lines: When the government tried to pass a law against early marriage, our people raised a tremendous howl.
If we do not stop it ourselves, he warns, the government will naturally intervene.
Parents give a ten-year-old daughter in marriage to a full-grown man. All the world cries fie upon us.
Is there any punishment without a sin? It is all the fruit of Karma, he says.

chapters.title: The courtship game
lines: In America, the struggle over marriage falls on the girls, not the parents. It is the girls' job to capture husbands.
He watches it all closely: I am, as it were, a woman amongst women.
Dinners, dances, musical parties, the watering places; and all the while the young women scheme how to capture husbands.
The boys flirt and slave for them, but the moment the girls reach out to catch them, they run away.
Money decides most matches, here as at home. One marriage in a thousand comes from love; then a quarrel, and divorce.

lines.q: It is the same in all countries. The result is the same in either case.

chapters.title: Since the Civil War
lines: Nowadays, he writes, American girls do not want to marry.
During the Civil War so many men were killed that women began to do all kinds of work, and they have kept the rights they won.

lines.q: If we truly fall in love, then we shall marry; otherwise, we shall earn and meet our own expenses.

lines: Even a millionaire's son must earn enough before he marries.
When a girl marries, she brings her husband into her parents' home.
And in everything the husband here must say, Yes dear.

chapters.title: Father or brother
lines: There are rivers of wealth here, he writes, waves of beauty, and an abundance of knowledge everywhere.
The women are sentimental, with a mania for romance.

lines.q: I am, however, a strange sort of animal who hasn't any romantic feeling.

lines: So they show him great respect. He makes them all call him father, or brother.
Of the unmarried girls, he says, they are exceedingly good, because their future is bright.

chapters.title: Lakshmi and Saraswati
lines: Many American women are very well educated, and put many a learned professor to shame.
And what kindness, what noble thought and action! In the best houses he is treated like their own son.
A young woman is gathering information about the weaving machine for him; the girls arranged a phonograph for the Maharaja of Khetri.

lines.q: They are the goddess Lakshmi in beauty and the goddess Saraswati in talents and accomplishments.

lines: This cannot be achieved through books, he says. Can you send out men and women to see the world?
The men here are clever at earning wealth. Where others do not see even dust, there they see gold.

chapters.title: Expansion is life
lines: Then he breaks into English.

lines.q: Keeping aloof from the community of nations is the only cause for the downfall of India.

lines: Since the English came, India has been forced back into the company of nations, and is visibly rising again.
Everyone who goes out of the country benefits the whole nation, for that is how its horizon expands. And because women cannot go, they have made almost no progress.

lines.q: There is no station of rest; either you progress upwards or you go back and die out.
The only sign of life is going outward and forward and expansion. Contraction is death.

lines: Why do good to others? Because it is the only condition of life: you expand beyond your little self, and live and grow.

lines.q: All narrowness, all contraction, all selfishness is simply slow suicide.

lines: Women too must go forward. Who would break this horrible crystallisation of death? Lord help us!

chapters.title: Patch the quilt slowly
lines: Yet change will come gradually, and he quotes a Bengali saying.

lines.q: One should cross a road slowly and cautiously; one should patch a quilt carefully and cautiously; so should one be slow and cautious in crossing a mountain.

lines: The papers from India have arrived, he reports, and the enemy has been silenced.
A fellow countryman, Mazoomdar, has been calling him a rogue, but no one pays attention.
These people let an unknown young man live among their families. I am like a foster son to the American women; they are really my mother.

chapters.title: Under a tree at Greenacre
lines: A while back, several hundred intellectual men and women gathered at a place called Greenacre, in Maine, and he stayed nearly two months.
Every day he sat in the Hindu fashion under a tree, and his followers sat on the grass all around him.
Every morning he taught them. How earnest they were!
The whole country now knows him. Some ministers are angry, though many learned ministers follow him.
I have been adopted by them, he writes.

chapters.title: A public man
lines: When will he return to India? Possibly next winter. There I shall have to wander, and here also I do the same.
Then a last request: please don't make this letter public.

lines.q: I have to be careful about every word I say. I am now a public man. Everybody is watching.

lines: Yours faithfully, Vivekananda.
